title: Repository management
text:
The gateway has to know whether a command reads or writes before it can choose a lock. classify sorts a Git argument list into one of three kinds. read commands, such as status and log, share a lock and run with --no-optional-locks, which stops Git from rewriting its index file in passing. write commands take the lock alone. net commands (clone, fetch, ls-remote and push) use a separate lock.
Some commands read or write depending on their arguments: git branch --list reads but git branch -d x writes. The MIXED table lists, for each such command, the arguments that make it a read. A command classify does not recognise counts as a write. That costs a little concurrency, but it means an unknown command that changes the repository never runs alongside another.


source


def classify(
    args
):
Classify a Git argument list as read, write, or net; unknown forms are writes.




source


def GitError(
    *args, **kwargs
):
Unspecified run-time error.



test_eq(classify(('status', '--porcelain=v1')), 'read')
test_eq(classify(('add', '--', 'x.py')), 'write')
test_eq(classify(('fetch', 'origin')), 'net')
test_eq(classify(('branch',)), 'read')                  # a bare `branch` lists
test_eq(classify(('branch', '-d', 'x')), 'write')
test_eq(classify(('branch', '--show-current')), 'read')
test_eq(classify(('config', '--get=x')), 'read')        # `--opt=value` is read by its stem
test_eq(classify(('config', 'user.name', 'x')), 'write')
test_eq(classify(('worktree', 'list')), 'read')
test_eq(classify(('worktree', 'add', 'x')), 'write')
test_eq(classify(('symbolic-ref', 'HEAD')), 'read')     # one argument reads, two write
test_eq(classify(('symbolic-ref', 'HEAD', 'refs/heads/x')), 'write')
test_eq(classify(('-C', '/tmp', 'status')), 'read')     # a global option, then the subcommand
test_eq(classify(('--no-pager', 'log')), 'read')
test_eq(classify(()), 'write')                          # unreadable, so pessimistic
test_eq(classify(('sneak',)), 'write')
test_eq(classify(('commit-tree', 'x')), 'read')         # writes an object, touches no ref

title: Repository management
text:
Locking one repository
RepoLock is a readers-writer lock: any number of readers at once, or one writer alone. The thread holding the write lock can take it again and can also read, so a change can inspect its own result without waiting on itself. The net lock is separate because network commands do not touch the index or the working tree.


source

RepoLock
def RepoLock():
A per-repository readers-writer lock, reentrant for the thread holding the write.



lock = RepoLock()
with lock.read():
    with lock.read(): pass                              # readers do not exclude each other
with lock.write():
    with lock.write(): pass                             # the writing thread is reentrant
    with lock.read(): pass                              # ...and may read inside its own write

seen = []
def reader():
    with lock.read(): seen.append('read')
with lock.write():
    t = threading.Thread(target=reader); t.start(); t.join(.2)
    test_eq(seen, [])                                   # a writer excludes a reader in another thread
t.join(2)
test_eq(seen, ['read'])

held = threading.Event()
def netter():
    with lock.net(): held.set(); time.sleep(.05)
t = threading.Thread(target=netter); t.start()
held.wait(2)
with lock.read(): pass                                  # ...but the network lock does not
t.join(2)

title: Repository management
text:
Recovery state
A Safepoint records where a repository was just before one change: the commit HEAD pointed at, the current branch, the commit holding a snapshot of uncommitted work (empty when there was none), how many files were uncommitted, the token that names it, and the time. Safepoints are kept as refs under refs/leela/safepoint/ and listed in a journal file inside .git. An ordinary push does not send either, so they stay on your machine. describe returns one line such as merge on main, 2 uncommitted file(s) kept.
SAFEPOINT_REF and JOURNAL_NAME still say leela, the editor this module was written for. Renaming them would lose track of safepoints already on disk.
FOREIGN_LOCK matches the errors Git prints when another process, such as a terminal or another editor, is holding one of Git’s lock files. The gateway retries those commands a few times, with a growing pause, before it gives up.


source

Safepoint
def Safepoint(
    token:str, op:str, head:str, branch:str, stash:str, dirty:int, created_at:int
)->None:
Where a repository was just before one change: its commit, its branch and a snapshot of uncommitted work.



p = Safepoint(token='a1', op='merge', head='abcdef1234', branch='main', stash='', dirty=0, created_at=0)
test_eq(p.describe(), 'merge on main')
test_eq(Safepoint('a1', 'rebase', 'abcdef1234', '', '', 0, 0).describe(), 'rebase on abcdef123 (detached)')
test_eq(Safepoint('a1', 'commit', '', '', '', 0, 0).describe(), 'commit on an unborn branch')
test_eq(Safepoint('a1', 'merge', 'abcdef1234', 'main', 'x', 2, 0).describe(),
        'merge on main, 2 uncommitted file(s) kept')

assert FOREIGN_LOCK.search("fatal: Unable to create '/r/.git/index.lock': File exists")
assert FOREIGN_LOCK.search('Another git process seems to be running in this repository')
assert not FOREIGN_LOCK.search('fatal: not a git repository')

title: Repository management
text:
The Git gateway
GitGateway runs Git commands under the right repository lock. The locks only protect anything if every caller shares one gateway, so use gateway() to get the process-wide instance rather than creating your own. The checks on this page create private gateways only so they can test them.
The gateway also caches, for some seconds, values that change less often than the files. memo(cwd, key, make, ttl) caches any value per repository. env_for lets an application choose the environment variables Git runs with in each checkout, for example to put the project’s virtual environment on PATH so Git can find a filter program installed there. When env_for is None, Git inherits the process’s environment. resolves finds the program a filter or hook command would run, using that PATH.


source

GitGateway
def GitGateway():
Run Git with shared repository locks, cached environments, and recovery journals.



gw = GitGateway()
r = mkrepo()
test_eq(gw._lock(r) is gw._lock(r), True)               # one lock per root, shared across callers
test_ne(gw._lock(r), gw._lock(mkrepo()))
assert gw._git().endswith('git')

calls = []
def make(): calls.append(1); return len(calls)
test_eq(gw.memo(r, 'k', make), 1)
test_eq(gw.memo(r, 'k', make), 1)                       # inside the ttl, the answer is not remade
test_eq(gw.memo(r, 'k', make, ttl=-1), 2)               # ...and outside it, it is
test_eq(gw.memo(r, 'other', make), 3)                   # keyed by (root, key)

test_eq(gw.env(r), None)                                # no `env_for` wired in: inherit the process
gw.env_for = lambda cwd: {'PATH': '/nowhere'}
test_eq(gw.env(r), {'PATH': '/nowhere'})
test_eq(gw.resolves(r, 'jupyter'), '')                  # not on that PATH
test_eq(gw.resolves(r, ''), '')
test_eq(gw.resolves(r, 'a "b'), '')                     # unparseable, not a crash
gw.env_for = None

title: Repository management
text:
Running a command
GitGateway.run is the only function in this module that starts Git. It takes the lock classify chooses, or the one named by kind, and runs the command with a 30 second timeout by default. When Git fails because another process holds one of its lock files, run tries again, up to four times in all, with a growing pause between tries. A failed command raises GitError, with both stderr and stdout in the message because Git prints useful text on either. With check=False it returns the failed result instead. out is run returning only stdout. Git’s stdin is input when given and /dev/null otherwise, so Git never shares the caller’s terminal.


source

GitGateway.out
def out(
    cwd, *args, **kwargs
):
Run one Git command and return its stdout.




source

GitGateway.run
def run(
    cwd, *args, check:bool=True, input:NoneType=None, timeout:int=30, kind:NoneType=None
):
Run one Git command in cwd under the repository’s lock, raising GitError on failure unless check=False.



gw, r = GitGateway(), mkrepo()
test_eq(gw.out(r, 'branch', '--show-current').strip(), 'main')
test_eq(gw.run(r, 'status', '--porcelain=v1').stdout, '')
test_eq(gw.run(r, 'rev-parse', 'nope', check=False).returncode != 0, True)   # check=False reports
test_fail(lambda: gw.run(r, 'rev-parse', 'nope'), contains='nope')           # ...and check=True raises
test_fail(lambda: gw.run(r, 'checkout', 'nope'), contains='did not match')

write(r, 'readme.md', 'changed\n')
test_eq(gw.out(r, 'status', '--porcelain=v1').rstrip(), ' M readme.md')
test_eq(gw.run(r, 'add', '-A', kind='write').returncode, 0)                  # an explicit kind wins
test_eq(gw.out(r, 'status', '--porcelain=v1').rstrip(), 'M  readme.md')

# stdin reaches the command, which is how a patch is applied.
test_eq(gw.run(r, 'hash-object', '-w', '--stdin', input='x\n').stdout.strip()[:2].isalnum(), True)
test_fail(lambda: gw.run(r, 'log', '--format=%H', timeout=0), contains='timed out')
# Without `input`, stdin is end of file, and a line waiting on the caller's terminal stays there.
import os, pty, sys
m, s = pty.openpty(); os.write(m, b'x\n')
probe = f"import os, select; from gheasy.repo import GitGateway; print(GitGateway().out({str(r)!r}, 'hash-object', '--stdin').strip(), os.read(0, 9) if select.select([0], [], [], 1)[0] else b'')"
got = subprocess.run([sys.executable, '-c', probe], stdin=s, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=60).stdout.split()
os.close(s); os.close(m)
test_eq(got, ['e69de29bb2d1d6434b8b29ae775ad8c2e48c5391', "b'x\\n'"])

title: Repository management
text:
Recording recovery points
The journal is a JSON file inside .git that lists safepoints newest first, keeping the latest JOURNAL_KEEP (60). It is written to a temporary file and renamed into place, so a reader never sees half a file. A journal that cannot be read or written never stops a Git command; one that cannot be read counts as empty.


source

GitGateway.journal
def journal(
    root
):
Safepoints for this repository, newest first.



gw, r = GitGateway(), mkrepo()
test_eq(gw._git_dir(r), r/'.git')
test_eq(gw._journal_path(r), r/'.git'/JOURNAL_NAME)
test_eq(gw.journal(r), [])                              # no file yet

for i in range(3): gw._record(r, Safepoint(f't{i}', 'op', 'a'*40, 'main', '', 0, i))
test_eq([p.token for p in gw.journal(r)], ['t2', 't1', 't0'])    # newest first

for i in range(JOURNAL_KEEP + 5): gw._record(r, Safepoint(f'x{i}', 'op', 'a'*40, 'main', '', 0, i))
test_eq(len(gw.journal(r)), JOURNAL_KEEP)               # capped, oldest dropped

gw._journal_path(r).write_text('not json')
test_eq(gw.journal(r), [])                              # unreadable reads as empty, never raises
gw._journal_path(r).write_text('[1, 2, {"token": "ok", "op": "o", "head": "h", "branch": "b", '
                               '"stash": "", "dirty": 0, "created_at": 0}]')
test_eq([p.token for p in gw.journal(r)], ['ok'])       # non-object rows are skipped

title: Repository management
text:
Creating a safepoint
safepoint captures uncommitted work with git stash create, which builds a stash commit without touching your files or adding to the stash list. It then points refs at that commit and at HEAD, so Git’s garbage collection keeps both. It returns None on a branch with no commits yet, where there is nothing to return to. transaction holds the repository’s write lock for a whole operation and records the safepoint before the operation starts.



transaction
def transaction(
    root, op, snapshot:bool=True
):
Hold the write lock for a whole operation, recording a safepoint first unless snapshot is false.




source

GitGateway.safepoint
def safepoint(
    root, op
):
Record where the repository is, without changing it, and return the Safepoint, or None on a branch with no commits.



gw, r = GitGateway(), mkrepo()
base = sh(r, 'rev-parse', 'HEAD')
write(r, 'readme.md', 'dirty\n')
p = gw.safepoint(r, 'demo')
test_eq((p.op, p.branch, p.dirty, p.head), ('demo', 'main', 1, base))
test_eq((r/'readme.md').read_text(), 'dirty\n')         # snapshotting does not clean the tree
assert p.stash
test_eq(sh(r, 'rev-parse', f'{SAFEPOINT_REF}/{p.token}/head'), base)
test_eq([x.token for x in gw.journal(r)], [p.token])    # ...and it is journalled

with gw.transaction(r, 'held') as point: test_eq(point.op, 'held')
with gw.transaction(r, 'held', snapshot=False) as point: test_eq(point, None)

title: Repository management
text:
Restoring a safepoint
undo first aborts any merge, rebase, cherry-pick or revert in progress. It then switches back to the recorded branch, resets it to the recorded commit, and reapplies the saved uncommitted work. Without a token it restores the newest safepoint.
If the saved work no longer applies cleanly, undo raises GitError, but the work stays reachable as a commit and the message gives the git stash apply command that recovers it. undo never discards that work. active_operation names the operation in progress, or returns an empty string.
gateway() returns the process-wide GitGateway.


source

gateway
def gateway():
Return the process-wide GitGateway.




source

GitGateway.active_operation

    root
):
Return the active Git operation name, or an empty string.




source

GitGateway.undo
def undo(
    root, token:str=''
):
Restore the safepoint named by token, or the newest one, including its uncommitted work.



gw, r = GitGateway(), mkrepo()
test_eq(gateway() is gateway(), True)
base = sh(r, 'rev-parse', 'HEAD')
write(r, 'readme.md', 'dirty\n')
p = gw.safepoint(r, 'demo')
commit(r, 'second', readme__md='second\n')

out = gw.undo(r)
test_eq((out['token'], out['restored'], out['op']), (p.token, 1, 'demo'))
test_eq(sh(r, 'rev-parse', 'HEAD'), base)               # back to where the safepoint said
test_eq((r/'readme.md').read_text(), 'dirty\n')         # ...with the uncommitted work reapplied

test_eq(gw.active_operation(r), '')
test_fail(lambda: gw.undo(r, 'nosuch'), contains='no safepoint nosuch')
test_fail(lambda: gw.undo(mkrepo()), contains='nothing to undo')

title: Repository management
text:
Finding and cloning repositories
repo_root returns the top folder of the checkout that contains a path, or None outside any repository. url_name gives the folder name a clone of a URL gets. clone_target works out where a clone would land and refuses anything risky: a URL starting with -, which Git would read as an option, a name containing /, a parent that is not a folder, or a target that already exists. clone makes the same checks, clones, and returns the new folder.


source

clone
def clone(
    url, parent, name:str=''
):
Clone url into parent, returning the new worktree root.




source

clone_target
def clone_target(
    url, parent, name:str=''
):
Where a clone of url would land, refusing anything but a free folder inside parent.




source

url_name
def url_name(
    url
):
The folder name a clone of url lands in: its last path segment, without .git.




source

repo_root
def repo_root(
    path
):
The containing worktree root, or None when path is not in a repository.



r = mkrepo()
write(r, 'src/app.py', 'x = 1\n')
test_eq(repo_root(r), r.resolve())
test_eq(repo_root(r/'src'), r.resolve())                # a folder inside
test_eq(repo_root(r/'src'/'app.py'), r.resolve())       # ...and a file inside
test_eq(repo_root(Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())), None)      # not a repository at all

test_eq(url_name('https://github.com/answerdotai/fastcore.git'), 'fastcore')
test_eq(url_name('git@github.com:answerdotai/fastcore.git'), 'fastcore')
test_eq(url_name('https://github.com/answerdotai/fastcore/'), 'fastcore')
test_eq(url_name(''), '')

parent = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()).resolve(); _tmp.append(str(parent))
test_eq(clone_target('https://h/o/thing.git', parent), parent/'thing')
test_eq(clone_target('https://h/o/thing.git', parent, 'other'), parent/'other')
test_fail(lambda: clone_target('', parent), contains='not a repository URL')
test_fail(lambda: clone_target('--upload-pack=evil', parent), contains='not a repository URL')
test_fail(lambda: clone_target('https://h/o/t.git', parent/'nope'), contains='not a directory')
test_fail(lambda: clone_target('https://h/o/t.git', parent, 'a/b'), contains='folder name')

test_fail(lambda: clone_target('https://h/o/taken.git', parent), contains='already exists')

A marker sequence with a part missing is left as ordinary text.

no middle

title: Repository management
text:
Short-lived status caching
An editor’s file tree can ask for the status of the same repository several times in one refresh. _cached shares one answer for _CACHE_TTL seconds, under half a second. invalidate(root) drops every cached answer for a repository, and each method that changes the repository calls it. An answer that was still being worked out when invalidate ran is not stored, so a stale result cannot slip back into the cache. changes, which an editor calls right after saving a file, never uses the cache.


source

invalidate
def invalidate(
    root
):
Drop every cached answer for root, after something wrote to it.



calls = []
def make(): calls.append(1); return len(calls)
root = '/some/root'
test_eq(_cached(root, 'k', make), 1)
test_eq(_cached(root, 'k', make), 1)                    # inside the ttl
test_eq(_cached('/other', 'k', make), 2)                # keyed by root as well as key
invalidate(root)
test_eq(_cached(root, 'k', make), 3)                    # a mutation drops what it invalidated
test_eq(_cached('/other', 'k', make), 2)                # ...and only that root
invalidate('/other')

title: Repository management
text:
Reporting outcomes
Every guarded change returns the same dictionary, described under “Mutation results” below, and _summarise turns it into one sentence for a person. A conflict comes first, because it is what needs dealing with, then an operation still in progress, then files staged but not yet committed.
_explain_filters explains filters that cannot run. A filter is a program, named in .gitattributes, that Git runs on a file as it is staged and checked out; nbstripout, which strips outputs from notebooks, is a common one.

base = {'op': 'merge', 'staged': [], 'conflicted': [], 'moved': False, 'head': 'abc1234',
        'message': '', 'operation': {'active': ''}}
test_eq(_summarise(base), 'merge changed nothing')
test_eq(_summarise(base | {'moved': True}), 'merge moved this branch to abc1234')
test_eq(_summarise(base | {'staged': ['a']}), 'merge staged 1 file without committing -- commit to finish')
test_eq(_summarise(base | {'operation': {'active': 'rebase'}}),
        'rebase is in progress -- continue, skip, or abort it')
test_eq(_summarise(base | {'conflicted': ['a', 'b']}),
        'merge stopped at 2 conflicted files -- resolve them to continue')
test_eq(_summarise(base | {'message': 'Already up to date.\nmore'}), 'Already up to date.')
# a conflict outranks everything else, because it is what the person has to deal with
test_eq(_summarise(base | {'conflicted': ['a'], 'staged': ['a'], 'moved': True}),
        'merge stopped at 1 conflicted file -- resolve them to continue')

assert 'cannot be found' in _explain_filters([{'name': 'nbstripout', 'configured': True,
                                               'clean': 'nbstripout', 'smudge': ''}])
assert 'configured nowhere' in _explain_filters([{'name': 'lfs', 'configured': False,
                                                  'clean': '', 'smudge': ''}])
test_eq(_explain_filters([]), '')

title: Repository management
text:
Reading a diff
Git’s machine-readable diff output separates fields with NUL characters and writes a renamed file as three fields rather than two, which a simple two-field parse gets wrong. _diff_status and _diff_numstat handle renames, and both keep None line counts for a binary file rather than reporting zero lines changed. _unified makes a unified diff of two strings, for files Git has no earlier version of.

test_eq(_unified_arg(3), '--unified=3')
test_eq(_unified_arg(-1), '--unified=0')                # clamped both ways
test_eq(_unified_arg(999), '--unified=20')

d = _unified('a\n', 'b\n', 'a/x', 'b/x')

Opening a repository
This is where the public API starts. GitRepo holds the root folder of one checkout, and every method from here on acts on it. GitRepo.at(path) accepts any path inside the checkout and raises GitError outside one. run runs any Git command in the repository and returns its stdout, for whatever the methods do not cover.
Four private helpers sit behind the methods. _ask returns stripped output, or an empty string when an optional read fails. _mutate runs a command and then clears the cache. _gitdir finds the .git folder, and _version reads a file as it is in the working tree, the index or HEAD.

title: Repository management
text:
Reading changes
changes lists every file that differs from the last commit. Each row has the path, the old path for a rename, Git’s one-letter status for the index and for the working tree, flags for staged, unstaged, untracked and conflicted, and line counts for the staged and unstaged parts. Untracked files are counted by reading them, since Git has no earlier version to compare with, and a binary file gets None counts.
changes always reads fresh state, because a caller that asks right after saving a file has to see the save. decorations returns the same rows through the short-lived cache, for a file tree that asks once per open folder in a single refresh.

The same rows as changes, through the short-lived cache, for a file tree that asks repeatedly.

title: Repository management
text:
What is in the way
Uncommitted changes to tracked files can stop a merge or a rebase from starting; untracked files usually do not. _in_the_way reports those changes in the form both previews return, so a preview can warn about them before you start.

r = GitRepo.at(mkrepo({'a.txt': 'a\n'}))
test_eq(r._blocking_changes(), [])
test_eq(r._in_the_way()['clean'], True)

write(r.root, 'a.txt', 'edited\n')
test_eq([c['path'] for c in r._blocking_changes()], ['a.txt'])
test_eq(r._in_the_way()['clean'], False)
test_eq(r._in_the_way()['dirty'], ['a.txt'])

sh(r.root, 'checkout', '--', 'a.txt')
write(r.root, 'untracked.txt', 'new\n')
test_eq(r._in_the_way()['clean'], True)                 # untracked work is not in the way

title: Repository management
text:
Preserving uncommitted work
Some operations need a clean working tree. _set_aside snapshots the changes to tracked files, keeps the snapshot under AUTOSTASH_REF, and resets the tree. _bring_back reapplies the snapshot after the operation.
Because the ref keeps the snapshot reachable, nothing is lost when it cannot be reapplied. In that case _bring_back leaves the operation’s result in place and returns a note with the command that recovers the work.

r = GitRepo.at(mkrepo())
test_eq(r._set_aside('demo'), '')                       # a clean tree has nothing to set aside

write(r.root, 'readme.md', 'mine\n')
oid = r._set_aside('demo')
assert oid
test_eq((r.root/'readme.md').read_text(), 'hello\n')    # the tree is clean again
test_eq(sh(r.root, 'rev-parse', f'{r.AUTOSTASH_REF}/demo'), oid)

test_eq(r._bring_back(oid), '')
test_eq((r.root/'readme.md').read_text(), 'mine\n')     # ...and the work comes back

# Work that cannot go back on top is kept as a commit, and the note says how to reach it.
r2 = GitRepo.at(mkrepo())
write(r2.root, 'readme.md', 'mine\n')
kept = r2._set_aside('demo')
commit(r2.root, 'moved on', readme__md='theirs\n')
note = r2._bring_back(kept)
assert 'git stash apply' in note and kept[:9] in note
test_eq((r2.root/'readme.md').read_text(), 'theirs\n')  # ...and the tree is left consistent

title: Repository management
text:
Mutation results
A merge that stops on conflicts has done its job; a person now resolves them. So _attempt returns normally when a command leaves conflicts or an operation in progress, and raises GitError for any other failure. _guarded wraps one risky change: it takes the write lock, records a safepoint, sets uncommitted work aside when asked, runs the change, brings the work back, and builds the result with _outcome.
That result is the dictionary every guarded method returns. It holds the operation’s name, Git’s message, the new and the old HEAD, whether the branch moved, the branch, the staged and conflicted files, any operation in progress, whether uncommitted work was carried across, the undo token with a description of what it undoes, and a one-sentence summary.

r = GitRepo.at(mkrepo())
test_eq(r._attempt('status', '--porcelain=v1'), '')
test_fail(lambda: r._attempt('checkout', 'nope'), contains='did not match')

before = sh(r.root, 'rev-parse', 'HEAD')
out = r._guarded('demo', lambda: r._attempt('commit', '--allow-empty', '-m', 'empty'))
test_eq(out['op'], 'demo')
test_eq(out['branch'], 'main')
test_eq(out['head_before'], before[:9])
test_eq(out['moved'], True)
test_eq((out['staged'], out['conflicted']), ([], []))
test_eq(out['operation']['active'], '')
test_eq(out['summary'], f"demo moved this branch to {out['head']}")
assert out['undo'] and 'demo on main' in out['undoes']
test_eq(gateway().journal(r.root)[0].token, out['undo'])

# A failure inside the guard still raises, and a safepoint is recorded before it does.
test_fail(lambda: r._guarded('bad', lambda: r._attempt('checkout', 'nope')), contains='did not match')
test_eq(gateway().journal(r.root)[0].op, 'bad')

# Work set aside for a mutation that fails is still brought back.
write(r.root, 'readme.md', 'mine\n')
test_fail(lambda: r._guarded('bad', lambda: r._attempt('checkout', 'nope'), autostash=True))
test_eq((r.root/'readme.md').read_text(), 'mine\n')

title: Repository management
text:
Listing branches
_branches reads every local and remote branch with one for-each-ref call, newest commit first, with its commit, upstream, how far it is ahead and behind, author and date. A remote branch that a local branch already tracks is left out, so main and origin/main do not appear as two entries. Each row also says whether the branch is merged into HEAD, whether it has the newest commit, and whether it is the remote’s default branch.

r = GitRepo.at(mkrepo())
rows = r._branches()
test_eq([b['name'] for b in rows], ['main'])
main, = rows
test_eq((main['current'], main['remote'], main['upstream']), (True, False, ''))
test_eq((main['ahead'], main['behind'], main['gone']), (0, 0, False))
test_eq((main['merged'], main['latest']), (True, True))
test_eq(main['subject'], 'initial')
test_eq(main['author'], 'Repo tests')

sh(r.root, 'branch', 'feature')
test_eq(sorted(b['name'] for b in r._branches()), ['feature', 'main'])

bare = mkbare()
sh(r.root, 'remote', 'add', 'origin', str(bare))
sh(r.root, 'push', '-u', 'origin', 'main')
commit(r.root, 'ahead one', readme__md='ahead\n')
rows = {b['name']: b for b in r._branches()}
test_eq(rows['main']['upstream'], 'origin/main')
test_eq((rows['main']['ahead'], rows['main']['behind']), (1, 0))
assert 'origin/main' not in rows                        # claimed by a local branch, so not shown twice

sh(r.root, 'push', 'origin', 'main:unclaimed')
sh(r.root, 'fetch', 'origin')
assert 'origin/unclaimed' in {b['name'] for b in r._branches()}

section: Filters that are configured and missing
text:
Filters that are configured and missing
A repository can name a filter in .gitattributes whose program is not installed where Git runs. Git does not treat a failing filter as an error, so the affected files show up as modified again however often they are staged. filter_health checks each filter named in .gitattributes, reports whether it is configured and whether its program can be found, and explains in plain words what is wrong.


source

GitRepo.filter_health

Whether this repository’s content filters can actually run.

sh(c.root, 'config', 'filter.nbstripout.clean', 'definitely-not-installed')

test_eq([b['name'] for b in health['filters']], ['nbstripout'])
test_eq((health['ok'], health['filters'][0]['configured']), (False, True))
test_eq(health['filters'][0]['resolved'], '')
assert 'cannot be found' in health['explain']

u = GitRepo.at(mkrepo({'.gitattributes': '*.bin filter=missing-test-filter\n'}))
health = u.filter_health()
test_eq([b['name'] for b in health['filters']], ['missing-test-filter'])
test_eq((health['ok'], health['filters'][0]['configured']), (False, False))
assert 'configured nowhere' in health['explain']

Staging

title: Repository management
text:
Switching branches
checkout switches to a local branch or a remote branch such as origin/feature. For a remote branch it creates a local branch that tracks it, or switches to the existing one and sets its upstream.
Git refuses to switch when the switch would overwrite uncommitted changes. checkout then sets the changes aside, switches, and puts them back. If they conflict with what is on the target branch, it switches back and restores the work, so you end up where you started with nothing lost.


source

GitRepo.checkout
def checkout(
    branch
):
Switch branches, setting aside uncommitted work only if Git refuses to carry it.



r = GitRepo.at(mkrepo())
assert r._has_ref('refs/heads/main')
assert not r._has_ref('refs/heads/nope')

sh(r.root, 'branch', 'feature')
out = r.checkout('feature')
test_eq(r.run('branch', '--show-current').strip(), 'feature')
test_eq(out['op'], 'checkout')
test_fail(lambda: r.checkout('nope'), contains='nope')

bare = mkbare()
sh(r.root, 'remote', 'add', 'origin', str(bare))
sh(r.root, 'push', 'origin', 'main:published')
sh(r.root, 'fetch', 'origin')
r.checkout('origin/published')
test_eq(r.run('branch', '--show-current').strip(), 'published')
test_eq(r._tracking()[0], 'origin/published')

# Uncommitted work the switch cannot carry leaves the repository exactly where it was.
r.checkout('main')
commit(r.root, 'diverge', readme__md='on main\n')
r.checkout('feature')
write(r.root, 'readme.md', 'in progress\n')
test_fail(lambda: r.checkout('main'), contains='you are still on feature with your work')
test_eq(r.run('branch', '--show-current').strip(), 'feature')
test_eq((r.root/'readme.md').read_text(), 'in progress\n')

# ...and work that has nowhere to clash comes across with it.
r.discard(['readme.md'])
write(r.root, 'scratch.txt', 'notes\n')
r.stage(['scratch.txt'])
r.checkout('main')
test_eq(r.run('branch', '--show-current').strip(), 'main')
test_eq((r.root/'scratch.txt').read_text(), 'notes\n')

title: Repository management
text:
Commit, and the remote
commit and pull are guarded and return the result dictionary; fetch and push return Git’s output as text. commit refuses an empty message, and amend=True replaces the last commit. fetch fetches from one remote or all of them, and by default prunes branches deleted on the remote. pull only fast-forwards. When your branch has commits the upstream lacks, it fails rather than making a merge commit you did not ask for; divergence and sync handle that case. push with publish=True pushes a branch that has no upstream yet and sets one, using origin when it exists. force_with_lease=True overwrites the remote branch, but only if nobody has pushed to it since you last fetched.

title: Repository management
text:

title: Repository management
text:
Replaying a branch in memory
A rebase rewrites history, so the only reliable way to know what one would do is to do it somewhere that does not count. _replay merges each of your commits onto the previous result with git merge-tree and wraps the result in a new commit with git commit-tree. Both only add objects to Git’s store and touch no branch, index or working tree, so the rehearsal leaves nothing you can see. It stops at the first commit that would conflict, which is where a real rebase would stop.
SYNC_OPS names the four ways sync can bring a branch level with its upstream, and REMOTE_OPS the three commands that talk to a remote.

test_eq(_short_commits([{'short': 'abc1234', 'subject': 'a subject'}]), ['abc1234 a subject'])
test_eq(_short_commits([{'short': 'a', 'subject': 'x'}] * 30), ['a x'] * 20)   # capped for a summary
test_eq(_said({'summary': 's'}), 's')
test_eq(_said({'message': 'm'}), 'm')
test_eq(_said(' text '), 'text')
test_eq(_said(None), '')
test_eq(sorted(SYNC_OPS), ['fast-forward', 'merge', 'rebase', 'reset'])
test_eq(REMOTE_OPS, ('fetch', 'pull', 'push'))

r = GitRepo.at(mkrepo({'a.txt': 'base\n'}))
test_fail(lambda: r._upstream(), contains='tracks nothing')
sh(r.root, 'branch', 'other')
commit(r.root, 'ours', b__txt='b\n')
onto = r._ask('rev-parse', 'HEAD')
r.checkout('other')
commit(r.root, 'theirs', c__txt='c\n')
head = r._ask('rev-parse', 'HEAD')

stops, replayed, files = r._replay(onto, list(reversed(r.history(ref=f'{onto}..HEAD'))))
test_eq((stops, replayed, files), (None, 1, []))        # replays cleanly
test_eq(r._ask('rev-parse', 'HEAD'), head)              # ...and moved nothing

c = GitRepo.at(mkrepo({'shared.txt': 'base\n'}))
sh(c.root, 'branch', 'other')
commit(c.root, 'ours', shared__txt='ours\n')
onto = c._ask('rev-parse', 'HEAD')
c.checkout('other')
commit(c.root, 'theirs', shared__txt='theirs\n')
stops, replayed, files = c._replay(onto, list(reversed(c.history(ref=f'{onto}..HEAD'))))
test_eq(stops['subject'], 'theirs')                     # the commit a rebase would stop at
test_eq((replayed, files), (0, ['shared.txt']))

title: Repository management
text:
Choosing a synchronization strategy
divergence compares the current branch with its upstream, or with a branch you name, and relation says how they stand: identical, ahead, behind or diverged. It then rehearses each way of bringing the branch level. A fast-forward is possible when you have no commits of your own, a merge or a reset whenever the upstream has commits you lack, and a rebase when both sides have commits. The merge is rehearsed with merge-tree and the rebase with _replay, so each option lists the files it would conflict on, and the options that rewrite history are marked destructive.
recommended is a fast-forward when you have no commits of your own. When both sides have commits, it is a rebase if your commits replay without conflict and nothing is uncommitted, and a merge otherwise. It is empty when the upstream has nothing you lack.


source

GitRepo.divergence
def divergence(
    upstream:str='', fetch:bool=False
):
You against your upstream, every way back rehearsed before any of them runs.



r = GitRepo.at(mkrepo({'a.txt': 'base\n'}))
bare = mkbare()
sh(r.root, 'remote', 'add', 'origin', str(bare))
sh(r.root, 'push', '-u', 'origin', 'main')
test_eq(r._upstream(), 'origin/main')

d = r.divergence()
test_eq(d['relation'], 'identical')
test_eq((d['ahead'], d['behind'], d['recommended']), (0, 0, ''))
test_eq(sorted(o['op'] for o in d['options']), sorted(SYNC_OPS))

other = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()); _tmp.append(str(other))
o = GitRepo.at(clone(str(bare), other, 'other'))
sh(o.root, 'config', 'user.email', 'tests@example.com')
sh(o.root, 'config', 'user.name', 'Repo tests')
commit(o.root, 'upstream moved', b__txt='b\n')
o.push()

r.fetch()
test_eq(r.divergence()['relation'], 'behind')
test_eq(r.divergence()['recommended'], 'fast-forward')

commit(r.root, 'we moved', c__txt='c\n')
d = r.divergence()
test_eq((d['relation'], d['ahead'], d['behind']), ('diverged', 1, 1))
test_eq(d['recommended'], 'rebase')                     # nothing rehearsed a conflict
test_eq({x['op']: x['available'] for x in d['options']}['fast-forward'], False)
test_eq({x['op']: x for x in d['options']}['rebase']['stops_at'], None)
test_eq(d['ours'], ['%s we moved' % r._ask('rev-parse', '--short', 'HEAD')])

Doing it

GitRepo.sync
def sync(
    how:str='rebase', upstream:str=''
):
Reconcile with the upstream the way divergence rehearsed.

o.push()

r.fetch()

test_fail(lambda: r.sync('sideways'), contains='sync must be one of')

test_eq(r.divergence()['relation'], 'ahead')

test_eq(r.divergence(fetch=True)['relation'], 'identical')

title: Repository management
text:
Ignore rules a folder needs
A folder without a suitable .gitignore stages build output such as target/, dist/, __pycache__ and node_modules along with the work. IGNORE_KINDS describes four kinds of project: Rust, maturin (a Python package built from Rust), Python and Node. For each it lists the files that mark a folder as that kind, paths that must end up ignored, and the rules to add when they are not. project_kinds says which kinds a folder holds.


source

project_kinds
def project_kinds(
    folder
):
Which kinds of project this folder holds, by the files that declare one.



d = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()); _tmp.append(str(d))
test_eq(project_kinds(d), [])
(d/'package.json').write_text('{}')
test_eq(project_kinds(d), ['node'])
(d/'Cargo.toml').write_text('[package]\n')
test_eq(project_kinds(d), ['rust', 'node'])             # marker order is `IGNORE_KINDS` order
(d/'pyproject.toml').write_text('[project]\n')
project_kinds(d)                                        # a crate plus a pyproject is maturin, not python

missing_ignores asks Git rather than guessing. It runs each kind’s probe paths through git check-ignore, so a .gitignore someone wrote by hand, in a different shape, still counts when it covers them, and the repository is left alone.


source

missing_ignores
def missing_ignores(
    repo, folder
):
The (kind, lines) this folder needs and the repository does not already cover.



r = GitRepo.at(mkrepo())
(r.root/'crate').mkdir(); (r.root/'crate'/'Cargo.toml').write_text('[package]\n')
test_eq([k for k, _ in missing_ignores(r, r.root/'crate')], ['rust'])
test_eq(_ignored(r, r.root/'crate'/'target'/'debug'/'build'), False)
write(r.root, '.gitignore', 'crate/target/\n')
test_eq(_ignored(r, r.root/'crate'/'target'/'debug'/'build'), True)
test_eq(missing_ignores(r, r.root/'crate'), [])         # already covered, in a shape of its own
test_eq(_ignored(r, '/elsewhere'), False)               # outside the worktree is never ignored
(r.root/'pyproject.toml').write_text('[project]\n')
missing_ignores(r, r.root)

prepare_ignores adds the missing rules to the folder’s own .gitignore, not the one at the repository’s root. A root rule /target/ does not match crate/target/, so rules written there for a crate in a subfolder would ignore nothing. A crate that carries its own ignore file also keeps it when moved into another repository. write=False reports what it would add without writing.
added is empty when the rules are already there, which is the usual case on a second run or in a checkout someone else set up.


source

prepare_ignores
def prepare_ignores(
    repo, folder, write:bool=True
):
Give folder the ignore rules its project kinds need, and say what was added.



r = GitRepo.at(mkrepo())
(r.root/'web').mkdir(); (r.root/'web'/'package.json').write_text('{}')
dry = prepare_ignores(r, r.root/'web', write=False)

text:
A folder can list repositories that are not under it, in a repos.txt file with one entry per line and # starting a comment. An entry is a path relative to the folder, an absolute path, or the URL the repository was cloned from. A URL stands for the folder a clone of it would have created, so the same list can be shared between people who have not all checked out everything; entries that are not checked out are skipped.
clone_url expands the short form such lists use: owner/name becomes a GitHub HTTPS URL, and anything else is taken to be a URL already.


source


def clone_url(
    spec
):
owner/name is the shorthand a list is written with; anything else is already a URL.



folder = mkfolder('alpha')
mkrepo(folder/'nested', 'deep')
(folder/MEMBERS).write_text('alpha  # the note after a repository\n# a whole line\n\nnested/deep\n')
test_eq(_members_file(folder), ['alpha', 'nested/deep'])
test_eq(_members_file(folder/'nowhere'), [])            # no list at all reads as an empty one

test_eq(_member_root('nested/deep', folder), folder/'nested'/'deep')
test_eq(_member_root('https://github.com/o/alpha.git', folder), folder/'alpha')
test_eq(_member_root('https://github.com/o/absent.git', folder), None)   # not checked out here

test_eq(clone_url('answerdotai/fastcore'), 'https://github.com/answerdotai/fastcore.git')
test_eq(clone_url('git@github.com:answerdotai/fastcore.git'), 'git@github.com:answerdotai/fastcore.git')
clone_url('https://github.com/answerdotai/fastcore.git')

title: Many repositories
section: The order they come back in
text:
The order they come back in
The order is fixed so that a list a person has learnt does not move under them: the open folder itself, then its direct children by name, then what its repos.txt names, then the folders another workspace added, with anything hidden dropped at the end. A repository reached twice is kept once, at its first position.


source

discover
def discover(
    roots, extra:tuple=(), hidden:tuple=()
):
Repository roots for a workspace of folders, in a stable, explainable order.



folder = mkfolder('beta', 'alpha')
mkrepo(folder/'nested', 'deep')                         # two levels down, so not a direct child
test_eq([p.name for p in discover([folder])], ['alpha', 'beta'])
(folder/MEMBERS).write_text('nested/deep\nalpha\n')
test_eq([p.name for p in discover([folder])], ['alpha', 'beta', 'deep'])   # `alpha` is already in

solo = mkfolder()
top = mkrepo(solo, 'top')
test_eq(discover([top]), [top])                         # an open folder that is itself a checkout
test_eq([p.name for p in discover([folder], extra=[top])], ['alpha', 'beta', 'deep', 'top'])
test_eq([p.name for p in discover([folder], hidden=[folder/'beta'])], ['alpha', 'deep'])
test_eq(discover([solo/'gone']), [])                    # a folder that is not there any more
discover([folder, top])

text:
The set a workspace lists
RepoSet is the open folders plus a small store file. The store remembers only the two things discovery cannot work out for itself: repositories a person added from outside the folders, and discovered ones they hid. The file is named after a hash of the folder paths, so two windows on the same folders share one list and a different set of folders gets its own. paths returns the list, and require returns one repository from it, raising GitError for a path the workspace does not list.
add lists a repository from outside the folders, or un-hides one. remove hides a discovered repository and forgets an added one. Nothing is ever deleted from disk.


source

RepoSet.remove
def remove(
    path
):
Drop a repository from the list. A discovered one is hidden; nothing is deleted.




source

RepoSet.add
def add(
    path
):
List a repository this workspace would not have found, and un-hide one it removed.




source

RepoSet.require
def require(
    path
):
The repository a caller named, refused unless this workspace already lists it.




source

RepoSet.paths
def paths():
Every repository this workspace lists.




source

RepoSet
def RepoSet(
    roots:list, store:Path=None
)->None:
The repositories a workspace lists, and the operations that mean something across all of them.



folder, away = mkfolder('alpha', 'beta'), mkfolder('solo')
ws = RepoSet([folder], state())
test_eq([p.name for p in ws.paths()], ['alpha', 'beta'])
test_eq(ws.require(folder/'alpha'), folder/'alpha')
test_fail(lambda: ws.require(away/'solo'), contains='not a repository in this workspace')

ws.add(away/'solo')                                     # from outside the open folders
test_eq([p.name for p in ws.paths()], ['alpha', 'beta', 'solo'])
ws.remove(away/'solo')
test_eq([p.name for p in ws.paths()], ['alpha', 'beta'])

ws.remove(folder/'beta')                                # a discovered one is hidden, not deleted
test_eq([p.name for p in ws.paths()], ['alpha'])
test_eq((folder/'beta'/'.git').is_dir(), True)
ws.add(folder/'beta')                                   # ...and adding it back un-hides it
test_eq([p.name for p in ws.paths()], ['alpha', 'beta'])
test_eq(ws._state(), {'hidden': [], 'extra': []})       # nothing discovery can work out itself
test_fail(lambda: ws.add(away), contains='not inside a Git repository')

title: Many repositories
text:
One row per repository
overview is the whole workspace as one table, with one brief row per repository and totals: how many are dirty, ahead, behind, on an unexpected branch, have commits since their last tag, or could not be read. expected_branch is the branch most repositories are on, unless you pass expect, and off_branch marks the rest. Repositories worked on together tend to drift onto different branches one at a time, and that is what a person needs to see first.
A repository that cannot be read becomes a row with an error rather than an exception, so one broken checkout does not blank the table.


source

RepoSet.overview
def overview(
    expect:str=''
):
Every repository as one row, plus what the workspace looks like as a whole.



folder = mkfolder('one', 'three', 'two')
(folder/'two'/'readme.md').write_text('edited\n')
sh(folder/'two', 'checkout', '-q', '-b', 'topic')
view = RepoSet([folder], state()).overview()
test_eq([r['name'] for r in view['repos']], ['one', 'three', 'two'])
test_eq([r['clean'] for r in view['repos']], [True, True, False])
test_eq(view['expected_branch'], 'main')                # what most of them are on
test_eq([r['off_branch'] for r in view['repos']], [False, False, True])
view['summary']

title: Many repositories
section: One operation across all of them
text:
One operation across all of them
run(op) runs one operation across every repository, or across the paths you pass. fetch, pull and push mean the same thing in every repository. Before running one, it checks each repository and reports in skipped when there is nothing to do, rather than running a command that would fail. A branch with no upstream is not an error; it is a branch nobody has published yet, and pull and push skip it.
status runs no Git command and returns one row per repository. It is there so a caller can use the same code for all four operations.


source

RepoSet.run
def run(
    op, paths:tuple=()
):
One operation across the named repositories, or across all of them.



folder = mkfolder('alpha', 'beta')
ws = RepoSet([folder], state())
test_fail(lambda: ws.run('rebase'), contains='unknown workspace operation')
test_eq([r['name'] for r in ws.run('status')], ['alpha', 'beta'])
test_eq([r['skipped'] for r in ws.run('push')], ['unpublished branch'] * 2)
test_eq([r['skipped'] for r in ws.run('pull')], ['no upstream'] * 2)
test_eq([r['output'] for r in ws.run('fetch')], ['up to date'] * 2)

bare = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()); _tmp.append(str(bare))
sh(bare, 'init', '-q', '--bare', 'origin.git')
sh(folder/'alpha', 'remote', 'add', 'origin', str(bare/'origin.git'))
sh(folder/'alpha', 'push', '-q', '-u', 'origin', 'main')
ws.run('pull', [folder/'alpha'])                        # ...and a published one has an upstream to ask about

text:
Cloning into the workspace
A clone has to land in a folder the workspace already watches, or it would not show up in the list. clone takes a list of URLs or owner/name entries and clones them into the first open folder, or into into. It refuses a folder outside the open folders, and reports each clone in its own row, so one bad name does not lose the others.


source

RepoSet.clone
def clone(
    urls, into:NoneType=None
):
Clone repositories into an open folder, in parallel, and say where each landed.



folder, source = mkfolder('alpha'), mkfolder('gamma')
ws = RepoSet([folder], state())
rows = ws.clone([str(source/'gamma')])                   # a local path is a URL git understands
test_eq([r['output'] for r in rows], ['cloned'])
test_eq([p.name for p in ws.paths()], ['alpha', 'gamma'])

test_fail(lambda: ws.clone([]), contains='at least one repository')
test_fail(lambda: ws.clone(['o/r'], into=source), contains='outside the open folders')
test_fail(lambda: RepoSet([], state()).clone(['o/r']), contains='open a folder to clone into')
ws.clone([str(folder/'not-here')])                       # one bad URL is one bad row

title: Many repositories
section: The repository a view is about
text:
The repository a view is about
An editor view that shows one repository needs to know which one. repo_for tries three answers in order: the repository it was told (target), which must be one the workspace lists; the chosen open folder, when that folder is itself a checkout; and otherwise the repository containing the open file (cwd).
The middle step is what makes a folder of checkouts work. A folder of clones is not a repository itself, so answering with it would make every Git view report “not a repository” while each file open inside it is in one. Falling through to cwd lets the view follow the open file from repository to repository. Outside any repository, repo_for returns cwd itself.


source

repo_for
def repo_for(
    roots, target:str='', chosen:NoneType=None, cwd:NoneType=None, store:NoneType=None
):
The repository a view is about: one this workspace lists, the chosen folder’s, or the open file’s.



folder, st = mkfolder('alpha', 'beta'), state()
solo = mkfolder(); top = mkrepo(solo, 'top')
test_eq(repo_for([folder], target=folder/'alpha', store=st), folder/'alpha')
test_fail(lambda: repo_for([folder], target=solo, store=st), contains='not a repository in this workspace')

test_eq(repo_for([top], chosen=top), top)               # an open folder that is itself a checkout
test_fail(lambda: repo_for([folder], chosen=folder), contains='open a folder first')
test_eq(repo_for([folder], chosen=folder, cwd=folder/'beta'/'readme.md'), folder/'beta')
repo_for([folder], cwd=solo)                            # outside every repository: the folder itself

title: Many repositories
text:
Finding one anywhere
find_repos finds repositories anywhere under a folder, for picking one out of a directory of checkouts that nobody has listed. query keeps those whose name or path contains it, and limit caps how many come back, sorted by name. It uses ripgrep when it is installed, because ripgrep walks a large tree much faster than Python, and falls back to os.walk otherwise. Both count depth the same way: how many folders below base the repository itself may be. Folders such as node_modules, virtual environments and caches are skipped.


source

find_repos
def find_repos(
    base, query:str='', limit:int=60, depth:int=6
):
Repositories anywhere under base, for picking one out of a directory of checkouts.



base = mkfolder('alpha', 'beta')
mkrepo(base/'nested', 'deep')
test_eq([p.name for p in find_repos(base)], ['alpha', 'beta', 'deep'])
test_eq([p.name for p in find_repos(base, 'de')], ['deep'])         # matched on name or path
test_eq([p.name for p in find_repos(base, depth=1)], ['alpha', 'beta'])
test_eq(len(find_repos(base, limit=1)), 1)
test_eq(find_repos(base/'nowhere'), [])
find_repos(base, depth=2)

text:
Trigger builder
Triggers are the events that start a workflow, and they go under on: in the YAML. Every WorkflowBuilder has a TriggerBuilder as its on attribute. Each trigger method adds one event and returns the trigger builder, so events chain: wfb.on.push(branches=['main']).pull_request(). Writing .on again partway along a chain is allowed and changes nothing. done returns to the workflow when the chain carries on with workflow methods.

Builder for a whole workflow: its name, triggers, workflow-wide settings and jobs.



Configuration
These set fields that apply to the whole workflow. run_name sets the title each run shows in the Actions tab, and may use expressions. permissions sets what the workflow’s GITHUB_TOKEN may do, with the value read, write or none for each scope. env sets variables for every job, and concurrency stops two runs in the same group from overlapping, cancelling the older one by default. job(job_id, needs=None) adds a job and returns it, and build() returns the finished WorkflowDoc.

Job presets
A preset adds a complete job in one call and returns the workflow builder, so presets chain one after another. uv_test_job checks out the code, installs uv, runs uv sync --frozen, and runs uv run pytest or the test_cmd you give; with python_versions it adds a matrix over them. uv_lint_job does the same setup and runs ruff. uv_pypi_job builds with uv build and uploads to PyPI through trusted publishing, which needs no API token but does need the project set up as a trusted publisher on PyPI. It runs only when a release starts the workflow, and waits for test unless you change needs. docker_job logs in to GHCR and pushes the image tagged latest, also after test. node_job, rust_job and go_job add a build-and-test job for those languages.
The job ids are fixed: test, lint, publish, docker, frontend, rust and go, so each preset can be used once per workflow.
wfb = Workflow('ci')
wfb.on.push(branches=['main'])
doc = wfb.uv_test_job().uv_lint_job().uv_pypi_job().build()

Recipes
A recipe returns a finished WorkflowDoc for a common whole workflow, ready to save. docker_build_push builds a Docker image on every push to the given branches and pushes it to GHCR, with tags chosen by docker/metadata-action. title: gheasy
text:
gheasy has four modules, and most projects only need one or two of them.
gheasy.workflow writes GitHub Actions workflows. A workflow is a YAML file under .github/workflows/ that tells GitHub which jobs to run on a push, a pull request or a release. You describe it with chained Python calls and gheasy writes the YAML, so you never have to get the indentation of a hand-written file right.
gheasy.core keeps a project’s CI settings in one file, .gheasy/config.json, and generates the workflow, git hooks, Git LFS rules and GitHub secrets from it. It also installs the gheasy command line tool.
gheasy.repo reads and changes a local Git checkout. Before any change that could lose work, such as a merge, a rebase or a reset, it records a safepoint: the commit the branch pointed at and a snapshot of your uncommitted changes. A single call puts everything back.
gheasy.repos works across many checkouts at once, for a folder that holds several repositories you work on together.

Generate a CI workflow
For a Python project that uses uv, uv_ci gives you a complete CI workflow in one call. It runs on every push and pull request to main, installs dependencies with uv sync --frozen, runs ruff, and then runs pytest. Passing lint_cmd=None, as here, leaves out the lint job. to_yaml returns the text, and save('.github/workflows/ci.yml') writes it to the place GitHub looks for it.

print(uv_ci("ci", lint_cmd=None).to_yaml())

name: ci
on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
  pull_request:
    branches:
      - main
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Setup uv
        uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v5
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: uv sync --frozen
      - name: Test
        run: uv run pytest

Inspect a local repository
GitRepo wraps one local checkout. GitRepo.at takes the repository root or any file or folder inside it, and finds the root itself. info returns everything an editor’s Git panel shows, in one dictionary: the current branch, how many commits it is ahead of and behind its upstream (the remote branch it tracks), the local and remote branches, remotes, uncommitted changes, tags, stashes, any merge or rebase in progress, whether the repository’s content filters can run, and recent safepoints. text:
Preview before changing history
A merge can stop on conflicts and a rebase rewrites your commits, so it helps to know what will happen before you run either. divergence compares the current branch with its upstream and tries a fast-forward, a merge, a rebase and a reset without performing any of them. It reports which are possible, which would conflict, and which it recommends. fetch=True fetches from the remote first, so the comparison is against the latest upstream. merge_preview and rebase_preview answer the same question for one branch you name.
None of these change your branches, the index or the files on disk. They use git merge-tree, which works out the result of a merge without checking anything out.

preview = repo.divergence(fetch=True)
preview['relation'], preview['recommended'], preview['options']

section: Change the repository with a way back
text:
Change the repository with a way back
The methods that can lose work record a safepoint before they run. These are checkout, commit, pull, merge, rebase, cherry_pick, revert, reset, sync, stash_pop and stash_apply. Each returns a dictionary with a one-sentence summary of what happened and an undo token. Passing the token to undo restores the branch, the commit and the uncommitted work as they were.
sync carries out one of the options divergence offered. The usual pattern is to call divergence, read recommended, and pass it to sync, as the last line here does.

result = repo.checkout('feature')
print(result['summary'])
repo.undo(result['undo'])

# Apply the strategy selected after reviewing `divergence`.
repo.sync(preview['recommended'])

title: gheasy
text:
Review branches and commits
review(base, head) shows what a branch changed: each file with its added and deleted line counts, the commits, and totals. It compares head with the merge base, the last commit the two branches share, so work that landed on base after the branch split off does not show up as part of the branch. Loading every file’s contents up front would be slow for a large branch, so review_file loads the two versions of one file, and the patch between them, only when you ask. commit_review and commit_file give the same view of a single commit compared with its parent.

review = repo.review('main', 'claude/ramabana-branching-review-uqj6v2')
review['summary'], review['commits']

file_review = repo.review_file('main', 'claude/ramabana-branching-review-uqj6v2', review['files'][0]['path'])
file_review['left'], file_review['right'], file_review['patch']

text:
Build a library pipeline
For anything uv_ci does not cover, start from Workflow(name), add triggers through .on, and add jobs. gheasy has one-call presets for the common jobs. Here uv_lint_job runs ruff, uv_test_job runs pytest once lint has passed, and uv_pypi_job builds the package and uploads it to PyPI once the tests have passed. build() turns the builder into a document you can print or save.
The publish job only runs when a GitHub release starts the workflow. This example triggers on pushes and pull requests alone, so add .release(types=['published']) to the triggers when you want releases to publish.

from gheasy.workflow import Workflow

wfb = Workflow("ci")
wfb.on.push(branches=["main"]).pull_request()
wfb.uv_lint_job()

title: gheasy
text:
Configure LFS and secrets
Git LFS keeps large binary files out of the Git history and commits a small pointer file in their place. gh_lfs installs LFS in the repository and tells it which file patterns to handle.
GitHub Actions jobs read their settings from secrets, which GitHub encrypts and hides in logs, and from variables, which are plain text. gh_push_env takes a dict of values and sends each key to one or the other, using the env_schema saved in .gheasy/config.json. A key whose schema default is None becomes a secret, and a key with a string default becomes a variable. Keys missing from the schema are skipped with a warning. It sets them with the gh command line tool, which must be installed and logged in.

from gheasy.core import gh_lfs, gh_secrets_from_file, gh_push_env, GheasyConfig

# 1. Track binary/media files in git-lfs
gh_lfs(['*.mp3', '*.ogg', '*.wav', '*.png', '*.jpg', '*.webp', '*.xml', '*.db'])

# 2. Describe the settings: a None default makes a secret, a string default makes a variable
cfg = GheasyConfig(app='vedicreader', env_schema={
    # variables (have sane defaults)
    'MODE': 'dev', 'PORT': '5001', 'DOMAIN': 'http://localhost:5001',
    'WANT_GOOGLE': 'true', 'WANT_GIT': 'false',
    'NEED_BACKUP': 'false', 'RC_TYPE': 's3', 'RC_PROVIDER': 'Cloudflare',
    # secrets (no default, so they must be set)
    'JWT_SCRT': None, 'RESEND_API_KEY': None,
    'GOOGLE_CLI': None, 'GOOGLE_SCRT': None,
    'CF_ACCESS_KEY_ID': None, 'CF_SCRT_ACCESS_KEY': None, 'CF_ENDPOINT': None,
})
cfg.save()

# sends each schema key found in the environment: None default -> gh secret set, string default -> gh variable set
import os
gh_push_env(dict(os.environ))

When every value should be a secret, you can skip the schema. gh_secrets_from_file reads the KEY=VALUE lines of a file such as .env, ignores blank lines and # comments, and sets each one as a GitHub secret. dry_run=True prints the gh commands instead of running them, and env='prod' limits the secrets to jobs that deploy to the prod environment.

# Push all KEY=VALUE pairs from .env as GitHub secrets
gh_secrets_from_file('.env')

# With dry-run to preview what would be pushed
gh_secrets_from_file('.env', dry_run=True)

title: gheasy
text:
Build a cross-package pipeline
A step can run any shell command, including Python that imports another package. This workflow uses dockeasy to write a Dockerfile, then builds the image and pushes it to GHCR, GitHub’s container registry. The paths filter means a push only starts it when one of the files that generate the Dockerfile has changed. workflow_dispatch adds a button to run it by hand from the repository’s Actions tab, and with_ sets an action’s inputs.

wfb = Workflow("Build caddy-sqlite image")
wfb.on.push(branches=["main"], paths=["dockeasy/proxy.py", "nbs/01_proxy.ipynb"])
wfb.on.workflow_dispatch()

wfb.job("build-and-push").runs_on("ubuntu-latest")\
    .permissions(contents="read", packages="write")\
    .checkout().end_step()\
    .setup_uv().end_step()\
    .step("Install deps").run("uv sync").end_step()\
    .step("Generate Dockerfile").run(
        'uv run python -c "\n'
        'from dockeasy.proxy import caddy_sqlite_dockerfile\n'
        'caddy_sqlite_dockerfile().save(\'Dockerfile\')\n'
        '"'
    ).end_step()\
    .step("Log in to GHCR").uses("docker/login-action@v3")\
        .with_(registry="ghcr.io",
               username="${{ github.actor }}",
               password="${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}").end_step()\
    .step("Build and push").uses("docker/build-push-action@v5")\
        .with_(context=".", push=True,
               tags="ghcr.io/vedicreader/caddy-sqlite:latest").end_job()

print(wfb.build().to_yaml())

name: Build caddy-sqlite image
on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
    paths:
      - dockeasy/proxy.py
      - nbs/01_proxy.ipynb
  workflow_dispatch:
jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Setup uv
        uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v5
      - name: Install deps
        run: uv sync
      - name: Generate Dockerfile
        run: "uv run python -c \"\nfrom dockeasy.proxy import caddy_sqlite_dockerfile\ncaddy_sqlite_dockerfile().save('Dockerfile')\n\
          \""
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - name: Build and push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/vedicreader/caddy-sqlite:latest

text:
Config
GheasyConfig is the contents of .gheasy/config.json as a Python object. Its app field holds the project name. envs holds one EnvConfig per place the app is deployed, such as prod or staging; each records the server’s host, the domain it serves, the branch that deploys there, and the app’s folder on the server. The remaining fields feed the generators further down. workflows and workflow_preset choose the CI jobs, test_cmd replaces pytest, deploy_cmd is the shell command a deploy job runs, extra_jobs holds custom jobs, env_schema decides which settings become secrets, and hooks and lfs set up the local repository.
add_env, set_lfs, set_hooks, set_workflows and add_job change the config and return it, so calls can be chained before save. load reads the file, and returns an empty config when there is none. from_pyproject starts a config named after the project in pyproject.toml.

text:
Generators
The mk_* functions turn a config into the contents of a file and return it as text; the gh_* functions further down write the files.
mk_deploy_job adds one environment’s deploy job to a Workflow builder. The job waits for test, runs only for pushes to that environment’s branch, writes the DEPLOY_KEY secret out as an SSH key, adds the server to known_hosts, and then runs the deploy command. The command is the cmd you pass, or the config’s deploy_cmd; with neither, it prints a warning and adds nothing.


source

    env_name, cfg, wfb, cmd:NoneType=None

Add the deploy job for env_name to the workflow builder wfb, or warn and add nothing when there is no deploy command.

text:
Workflow generation
mk_workflow builds the whole CI workflow for a config and returns it as YAML text, headed by a comment saying gheasy manages the file. Which jobs it includes is decided in three layers, each overriding the one before: the preset named in workflow_preset, the flags in cfg.workflows, and the keyword arguments you pass. A preset only switches on a language job: rust and go turn on the job of the same name, fastapi-react and nodejs turn on node, and python and fasthtml turn on nothing.








Flag
Job
What it runs




test
test
uv run pytest, or uv run followed by cfg.test_cmd


lint
lint
ruff check and ruff format --check


publish_pypi
publish
uv build and a PyPI upload, only when a release starts the workflow


docker_build
docker
builds the image and pushes it to GHCR


node
frontend
npm ci, npm run build and npm test


rust
build
cargo build, cargo test and cargo clippy


go
build
go build, go test and go vet


on_pull_request
none
runs the workflow on pull requests as well as pushes



The publish and docker jobs wait for test, so keep test on when you use them. The workflow runs on pushes to the branches named in cfg.envs, or to main when there are no environments. Each environment gets a deploy job from mk_deploy_job, and the custom jobs in cfg.extra_jobs are added last. gh_workflow writes the result to .github/workflows/gheasy.yml. Regenerate that file rather than editing it, because the next regeneration overwrites hand edits.

def mk_workflow(
    cfg, *, on_pull_request:bool | None=None, # also run on pull requests, not only pushes
    test:bool | None=None, # uv test job: `uv run pytest`, or cfg.test_cmd
    lint:bool | None=None, # ruff check and format check
    publish_pypi:bool | None=None, # PyPI trusted publishing on release events, after test
    docker_build:bool | None=None, # Docker build and push to GHCR, after test
    node:bool | None=None, # `frontend` job: npm ci, build and test
    rust:bool | None=None, # Rust build, test and clippy
    go:bool | None=None, # Go build, test and vet
):
Build the CI workflow YAML for cfg; a flag left as None takes its value from the config’s preset and workflows.



# deploy skipped when no deploy_cmd
cfg_no_deploy = GheasyConfig(app='myapp')
cfg_no_deploy.add_env('prod', '1.2.3.4', 'myapp.com')
wf_str = mk_workflow(cfg_no_deploy)
assert 'deploy-prod' not in wf_str
assert '# Managed by gheasy' in wf_str

# deploy included when deploy_cmd set
cfg = GheasyConfig(app='myapp', deploy_cmd='./deploy.sh')
cfg.add_env('prod', '1.2.3.4', 'myapp.com')
wf_str2 = mk_workflow(cfg)
assert 'deploy-prod' in wf_str2

# explicit flag=True overrides cfg (no flags in cfg, test=True via kwarg)
wf_test = mk_workflow(cfg, test=True)
assert 'uv run pytest' in wf_test
assert 'jobs:\n  test:' in wf_test or 'test:' in wf_test

# explicit flag=False suppresses even if cfg would enable it
cfg_with_test = GheasyConfig(app='myapp', workflows={'test': True})
cfg_with_test.add_env('prod', '1.2.3.4', 'myapp.com')
cfg_with_test.deploy_cmd = './deploy.sh'
wf_notests = mk_workflow(cfg_with_test, test=False)
assert 'uv run pytest' not in wf_notests

# lint + test via kwargs
wf_lint = mk_workflow(cfg, test=True, lint=True)
assert 'ruff' in wf_lint
assert 'needs: test' in wf_lint or 'needs: test' in wf_lint.replace("'", "")

# on_pull_request adds pull_request trigger
wf_pr = mk_workflow(cfg, on_pull_request=True)
assert 'pull_request:' in wf_pr

# workflow_preset='rust' enables rust job by default
cfg_rust = GheasyConfig(app='myrust', workflow_preset='rust')
wf_rust = mk_workflow(cfg_rust)
assert 'dtolnay/rust-toolchain' in wf_rust

print('mk_workflow OK')

text:
Local Git setup
The next functions change files inside your checkout: hook scripts in .git/hooks/ and the LFS block in .gitattributes.

title: core
text:
Git hooks
A git hook is a script Git runs at a fixed moment, such as pre-commit, which runs just before each commit and can stop it. gh_hooks installs hooks from a dict of hook name to command, where a command is a string or a list of lines. Without a dict it uses hooks from the config. It writes each script into .git/hooks/ between gheasy’s markers and makes it executable. Running it again replaces only the marked block, so anything you wrote above or below it stays.
nbdev_hook returns the usual command for an nbdev project, uv run --with nbdev nbdev-prepare, which exports, tests and cleans the notebooks before every commit. gh_githooks_pre_commit installs that command, or the one you pass, as the pre-commit hook.
Git never commits the contents of .git/hooks/, so these hooks stay on your machine and each new clone needs them installed once. gh_setup and GheasyRepo.new do that for you. When hooks have to be shared across many repositories, or are written in several languages, the pre-commit package is the better tool.


source

gh_githooks_pre_commit
def gh_githooks_pre_commit(
    cmd:NoneType=None, path:str='.'

text:
LFS and .gitattributes
Large binary files such as model weights and databases make a repository slow to clone, because every version stays in the history. Git LFS stores them on a separate server and commits a small pointer file in their place. gh_lfs runs git lfs install, then git lfs track for each pattern, and saves the patterns to the config. Without patterns it tracks a default list: *.db, *.onnx, *.bin, *.pt, *.pkl, *.safetensors, *.tar.gz, *.mp4 and *.parquet.
gh_gitattributes rewrites the gheasy block in .gitattributes from the patterns in the config and leaves every other line alone, so attributes you added yourself, such as *.sh text eol=lf, survive. Run it after changing the patterns in the config.

gh_gitattributes()                           # after any change to the patterns in the config

text:
Secrets and variables
GitHub Actions jobs read their settings from two stores. A secret is encrypted and hidden in logs; a variable is plain text. gh_secret sets one secret with gh secret set. With env='prod' it scopes the secret to the GitHub environment prod, so only jobs that deploy there can read it. gh_secrets_from_file sets every KEY=VALUE line of a file such as .env as a secret. Use gh_push_env when some values should be variables: it takes a dict and uses the config’s env_schema to choose, sending a key whose schema default is None to the secrets and a key with a string default to the variables. All three accept dry_run=True, which prints the gh commands instead of running them.
gh_deploy_key_setup uploads an SSH private key as the DEPLOY_KEY secret that the deploy jobs from mk_deploy_job use to reach the server. Two steps come first and are yours to do: create the key pair with ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f deploy_key, and add the public key to the server’s ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.

text:
The pull request a branch belongs to
An editor’s status line wants to say whether the current branch has an open pull request on GitHub and how it stands. pr_context(path, branch) answers that. It returns the pull request’s number, title and link, the branch it targets (its base), whether it is a draft, GitHub’s merge state, how many commits the branch is ahead of the base and how many the base has gained since the branch split off, and the total, failing and pending checks on the branch’s latest commit. The answer is cached for a minute, because a status line asks far more often than a pull request changes.
pr_context never raises. When there is no open pull request, no GitHub remote, no token, or GitHub refuses the request, pr is None and note says why. The example below runs _checks, the part that counts checks, against a fake API.

gh_check audits a repository against gheasy’s defaults and returns a list of findings. In the checkout it looks for gheasy’s pre-commit hook, for the LFS block in .gitattributes, and for a pyproject.toml that builds with hatchling.
